summary.text: The front matter of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, with cataloguing data, joint copyright and ISBNs for both organizations. It includes the foreword, acknowledgements and an overview of the toolkit's three parts on developing a national eHealth vision, an action plan and a monitoring framework. It ends with tables of contents and lists of figures and tables.

blocks.title: National context for eHealth
blocks.content:
1.1	 The case for eHealth1
eHealth is changing health-care delivery today and is at the core of responsive health systems. 
The daily business of health relies on information and communication and, increasingly, on the 
technologies that enable it, at every level and in every country. This is equally so in delivering 
care, deploying personnel, managing programmes or conducting research. 
The World Health Organization defines eHealth as the use of information and communication 
technologies (ICT) for health2. In its broadest sense, eHealth is concerned with improving the 
flow of information,

summary.text: Opens the chapter on national context by making the case for eHealth as central to responsive health systems and giving WHO's definition of eHealth as the use of ICT for health. It describes how eHealth supports care delivery, workforce, programme management and research. It notes international commitments to eHealth and the need for national strategies to coordinate efforts.

blocks.title: Framework for a national eHealth vision
blocks.content:
Chapter 2
Framework for a national eHealth vision
A national eHealth vision explains why a national approach to eHealth is needed, what a 
national eHealth plan will achieve, and how it will be done (Figure 3). Answering these 
questions constitutes the major work of strategy development.

blocks.content:
method
The Toolkit method is based on experience and lessons from countries that have already 
developed a national strategy (Figure 4). A successful outcome requires effective leadership, a 
well-managed process and stakeholder engagement. The vision is developed through an iterative 
approach, which ensures it is grounded in the current context, yet is not overly constrained.

Annex A 
Results-based management
Results-based management (RBM) has become increasingly important for the United Nations 
and its specialized agencies as they have sought to improve their ability to respond to new 
demands within the limits of resource constraints, and to demonstrate that they have delivered 
on expectations. It is also of direct relevance to the establishment of monitoring and evaluation 
for a national eHealth programme.
